04 / Pipeline map

What the solver actually has to do.

Reusable preparation produces factor-base logs. The online solve consumes one new public point and includes every target-dependent attempt through independent scalar verification.

Reusable preparation Cost and memory reported separately
  1. 1Build the factor baseChoose exact subgroup points and declare sign / Frobenius orbit folding.
  2. 2Find and verify relationsOrdinary queries → point decomposition → verified, useful matrix rows.
  3. 3Solve the relation matrixCheck rank and recover verified factor-base logarithms.
One target · primary online clock Start at target-dependent work → stop after independent verification
  1. 4Decompose the targetGenerate queries, encode and solve. Charge failed and timed-out attempts.
  2. 5Recover its logarithmCheck the relation, perform target descent and combine the known factor logs.
  3. 6Verify the answerIndependently check that the recovered scalar maps the generator to this target.
Factor bases & Frobenius orbits

Record the actual usable point set before folding, then folded columns and final rank separately. Different bases are different complete candidates even when their counts match.

PDP: F4 / F5 / SAT

PDP means point decomposition. Its internal polynomial or Macaulay matrix belongs to this stage. Solvers must return a verified point relation, not merely a satisfiable encoding. Every inconclusive attempt stays visible.

Final linear algebra & descent

The final relation matrix is distinct from the solver’s internal matrix. Rank, modular arithmetic, recovered logs, recursive target work and the final scalar check all need evidence.

Rho must solve the same one point with the same resource limits. Fixture generation, process launch and input loading are outside both online intervals. A missing phase cost remains unknown.

05 / Tournament design

A local win is a candidate, not a final answer.

01 / EXPLOREKeep diverse candidates

Different bases, solver families and stage combinations. Preserve alternatives with different resource tradeoffs.

02 / ADMITPass correctness gates

Source identity, natural yield, failed attempts, complete costs and verified recovered answers.

03 / COMPAREPair frozen workloads

Same fresh point, resources and reference. Screening and untouched confirmation have separate roles.

04 / DECIDEPromote or retain

Apply the declared uncertainty gate. Keep negative outcomes and useful alternatives for later combinations.

Next gate
Produce both native natural-yield records.

Use each exact pipeline, retaining failed attempts. Then freeze new target exclusions, calibrated resources and strong references before a fresh paired tournament. The three historical confirmation sets remain closed.

This diagram describes the proposed process. It does not claim that a fresh F5/SAT tournament has run, or that any implementation is globally fastest.

    How new results update this dashboard

    How this page stays current / AGENTS.md §7a

    Every result lands here in the pull request that produces it.

    States the rule since 3 October 2026: a pull request landing a measurement, reclassification, corrected reference or withdrawn claim updates every panel citing that kind of result before it merges.

    Rule since 3 October 2026 · checked in CI

    This dashboard is the first thing a reader opens, so a stale panel is worse than none. Since 3 October 2026 the repository’s agent rules (AGENTS.md §7a) make the update part of the result: a pull request that lands a new measurement, a reclassification, a corrected reference or a withdrawn claim must update every panel that cites that kind of result before it merges, and the finish-and-merge authorization does not cover a pull request that skips this.

    Which panels a result owes, by kind. The newest verified figure in each regime is shown; the figure it supersedes stays as “was”.
    Result kindPanels that must change
    Any IC / rho ratio, cold or online, elliptic or notThe progress chart: a new point in its series, dated the day the pull request merges, with reference quality, class, anchor and source
    A new best in any regimeThat row of the best-of table, the old figure kept as “was”; a new regime is a new row
    A cross-method ecbench sessionThe every-candidate panel or a new panel in its unit, and a chart point for its best cold one-target IC cell
    A tournament or autolab roundThe round’s own panel, the reference history where the reference changed, and the chart
    A boundary, exponent or phase priced for the first timeThe exponent panel and the boundary facts
    A verdict changeThe sentence at the top of this page and the first row of the best-of table

    What makes it checkable: the progress chart’s data is one file, docs/ic/progress-timeline.json, and the site build test fails when the copy embedded here differs from it, when a point has no row in the plotted-point table, or when the file’s date is older than its newest point. One point per result, not per pull request; dates are merge dates. GitHub Pages republishes this page from main on every merge, and any other published copy is republished from the canonical file in the same task or named as stale. Reviewing a pull request means reading its dashboard diff against the result’s own frozen files: every number here is the number in the session, table or report it links to, and nothing on the page is computed from another number on the page.

    Open the full historical ledger
    Cryptanalysis cost ledger · aburan28/crypto

    Index Calculus Scoreboard

    In plain terms

    The question. Can index calculus, a family of algebraic attacks, solve the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm faster than Pollard rho, the generic method every curve is sized against? Every panel on this page is one measurement of that question, with every phase of the attack counted, on a planted or public logarithm that was then checked.

    The answer so far: no. Priced end to end, no elliptic-curve row on this page is below rho. The closest are 3.6× slower on a 39-bit Koblitz subgroup when 32 targets are solved together, 13.5× on a 23-bit prime-field curve and 38.2× on a 24-bit random binary curve. Under the current one-target rule the Koblitz method finishes its online phase 8.8–17.5× faster than rho, but only after a reusable set-up that makes it 4.9–31.6× slower cold, and that same set-up would speed up a generic walk too. The gap widens as curves grow: no fitted exponent sits below rho’s. Every route tried against ECC2K-130 is bounded above rho or closed. Nothing here threatens a deployed curve.

    The one exception is not an elliptic curve: on hyperelliptic Jacobians of genus 4, at toy sizes (p ≤ 251), index calculus measures below rho, 0.24 at N = 224. That is a statement about the shape of the cost curve, not about any deployed system.

    How to read a row. S is the whole attack’s cost in one unit, scaled so that rho reads about 1 at every size; smaller is better. vs rho is the ratio to the matched rho on the same instance; above 1, rho wins. vs floor is the ratio to the provable lower bound for a generic method. The class chip says what a change meant: advance moved the ratio to the floor, which is the only kind of progress; engineering made the code cheaper without changing the mathematics; accounting changed only the bookkeeping; and relabelling lowered a headline number while the real cost rose.

    Why the page is so long. It is a ledger, not a summary. Negative results, corrections and superseded figures stay on it by rule, with the old value kept as “was” beside the new one, so that an improvement in the code is never mistaken for an improvement in the attack. The sections below are in the order the work was done. Historical panels are collapsed to their titles, each with a one-line summary beneath it: click a title to open one, follow a link into it, or use expand all below. The panels the current verdict rests on stay open.

    accounting Volcano metadata correction: Frobenius-order conductors are now distinct from certified endomorphism conductors; unknown strata remain unknown. Historical volcano labels are superseded. Correction and regression fixtures. Bounded exhaustive validation: 7,968 curve models and 9,984 capped neighborhoods; three correctness defects corrected, no ECDLP speedup measured. No ECDLP performance gain or ratio to rho is claimed.

    The calibrated index-calculus families below are scored against their generic-group floor and matched Pollard rho reference. The residual-walk thread's hundreds-of-times-behind-rho verdict on E(Fp3) is unchanged (its best cell is now the j = 0 orbit quotient of the subspace base at 224× plain rho, 388× a rho folded by the same automorphism, an engineering step from 898 to 312; the one route whose distance to parity is a constant, Joux–Vitse three-point decompositions at k = 4, measures 6,945× rho flat from 232 to 240, and the rho-parity ledger shows every measured route bounded away from parity below 2151). In the three-regime whole-pipeline ledger that heads the page, none of its elliptic-curve rows is below rho: its best rows are 13.5× the matched rho on a 23-bit prime-order curve, 38.2× on a 24-bit random binary curve and 3.6× was 4.3× on a 39-bit Koblitz subgroup, with no fitted exponent below the reference's. The Koblitz figure read 1.17× after the collection and selection rounds of 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-22 until ledger §19 (2026-09-23) matched its reference to its problem: it is 32 targets solved together, per target, and it had been divided by rho solving one. Against batch rho on the same 32 targets it is 6.5×; priced by time on both sides — rho’s canonicalisation each step, the pair table’s two passes each stored pair — 6.4×; one target alone, 44×. Ledger §20 (2026-09-26) re-priced it on current main with every phase on the clock, and that same recipe reads 12.5×. Its descent had been charged 54 units where it scans 748,180, and the workflow’s constructions around it had not been charged at all. The thread’s best recipe, swept at each of nine sizes from 218 to 247.2, reaches 4.9× at 239 and no lower. Ledger §21 (2026-09-26) then built the workflow’s constructions once per base, with every count unchanged. That makes the whole pipeline 1.04–2.25× faster and takes the same row to 4.3×. On current main, which later rounds made 12–33% cheaper at the top, ledger §22 (2026-09-30) cut the descent’s fixed cost per target: 1.35–1.39× at the small end in isolated runs, and the row reads 3.6×. Under AGENTS.md’s IC measurement rules (#1076, 2026-09-30) that figure, like every k = 32 ratio on this page, is a historical multi-target diagnostic. The primary comparison is now one unseen target against rho on the same point, with the reusable set-up reported apart. Ledger §23 (2026-10-01) measured it on 384 public points at the thread’s six largest sizes, 236.6–247.2. Online the descent is 8.8–17.5× faster than rho on the same point, or 4.3–9.4× with rho’s step at the canonical price. But it needs a reusable set-up that makes the method 4.9–31.6× slower cold (2.0× at 238.0, where both arms pay a slow curve construction). By Bernstein and Lange’s trade-off, a model, the same set-up spent as a generic precomputation would be 2.0–8.0× faster online still (the round). At baseline v3 (2026-10-06), after the ic tool programme’s rounds and main’s carry-less folds, the same comparison on 408 rows reads 10.2–26.5× faster online and 5.2–21.0× slower cold: rho is still faster cold at every size, and the gap still grows with the size (the programme). The first two were 3.55× and 16.0× until the reference was matched (ledger §18, 2026-09-23): the prime and binary rows had been priced against a walk that used no automorphism and paid most of its S in set-up, and against the negation-map walk the contract asks for they read 2.4–3.8× higher — an accounting change that moves no index-calculus count and makes the verdict below stronger. Before that, two independent things moved those numbers and they must not be confused. Round 5 read lower than Round 4’s 3.63 and 21.9 for a reason that is not progress and is not counted as any: it re-seeded the walk rows, which moves a single row by up to a factor 1.8 in either direction at three repeats, and its own lever is exactly 1.000× on all three (see the panel below). That same re-seed took the Koblitz row from 30.3× to 26.1×. The collection and selection rounds behind the 6.5× are real progress between index-calculus variants — 7.26× fewer operations than the rung they started from, every phase priced — but their distance to rho was read against the wrong reference, which is the mistake the repository’s own multi-target rule warns about: a batch win over single rho measures the baseline. The correction is accounting and is almost entirely the batch: batch rho at k = 32 costs 0.19–0.22 of its single-target floor per target, as the Kuhn–Struik law predicts, and the thread’s single-target walk had also sat 1.2–1.8× above that floor. The rounds also drove the relation count to its counting floor, so that lever is spent rather than promising. Round 3 turns the general statement from a report into a boundary. The pair-table family has a derived shape law — a two-summand row pays F²/4t for its table and about c·#E/(2kF) for its relations, least at F = (c·#E·t/k)1/3 — and in this unit, where rho is a constant, that optimum is 0.75 r1/6 on a prime-order curve. A constant and an unbounded increasing function cross once, at r ≈ 22. Neither the base size, the two folds, the summand count nor the relation count changes that: for a row needing K1−a relations the optimum is r2/(3+a)−1/2, positive for every a < 1. So this family has no crossover to find at any size, and at sect163k1's size it sits about 107× the automorphism-aware walk it competes with. That r1/6 rise was also read as a measured crossing. The tournament collector that sat strictly below rho on an eight-cell Koblitz panel reads 0.831 [0.772, 0.894] at r = 4.2×106 and 1.533 [1.238, 1.899] at r = 2.3×108, both bands clear of one in opposite directions, and beyond the crossing the ratio grows at r[0.13, 0.19] across three certified cells and 1100× in r (below). But that crossing was measured against the tournament worker’s rho, which is not a matched reference. Its step spends about 9,100 of 9,930 instructions naming Frobenius classes by squaring, a cost the IC arm had engineered away. Given the IC arm’s own orbit naming, that rho beats the lane’s IC pipeline at every cell measured: by 1.19–2.88×, from r = 4.2×106 to 1.2×1010 (below). So no crossing with a matched rho has been measured, and the r[0.13, 0.19] is a growth against the unmatched walk. That tournament line was stopped on 2026-09-29 (reference history; decision). Against a rho in the IC arm’s own arithmetic, no collector is below rho in instructions at any of twelve cells. Its one lead is 16–26% in isolated in-process time at n ≤ 19, gone by 23. That is engineering: it comes from more instructions per second, not fewer instructions, and a rho with its cache sized to the walk removes it: IC is within 0.98–1.03 of that rho in wall time at the four small cells, and 4% behind it at n = 23. The two symmetry levers left untested are now settled at m = 3: Frobenius-orbit coordinates are closed by structure, and the summand-symmetric Riemann–Roch norm form reads a degree slope of 1.17 per unit ℓ (constant lever); the Riemann–Roch route is closed for the exponent at these sizes in each of its algebraic forms. An independent Gröbner engine (Singular’s degree-truncated slimgb) confirmed every in-tree reading of that ladder and extended it one rung: the direct S4 descent refutes at degree 10 at ℓ = 5, three above the sharp first-fall bound and still rising one per rung, and the next rung is out of memory at 12 GB (external-engine ladder). The m = 4 algebraic audits read ĉ ≈ 1.0 against the 0.25 needed, on both engines. The derived exponent lies inside that range — but at a factor base measurably not where the same derivation puts it, so the agreement is not yet confirmation of the model. Carried from §19’s 6.38×, the same rise predicted that the Koblitz collection thread crosses batch rho near 223. Measured at nine sizes with every phase priced (§20), it does not, and building its constructions once (§21) and cutting its descent’s fixed cost (§22) does not change that. The thread reads 7.0–14.9× was 9.7–20.9× below 225, where its descent, which no number of targets amortises, still costs more per target than batch rho does. Its least ratio is 3.62× was 4.28× at 239. Above that the ratio rises again. On current main the declared fit gives r0.137, 95% [−0.06, 0.33]: the rise is not resolved from zero, and it is not separated from 1/6. That bounds the tabled family only; an algebraic decomposition oracle builds no such table and its asymptotics are the question this ladder cannot reach. It is also not blanket across problems: on hyperelliptic Jacobians at genus 2, 3 and 4 index calculus measures below a real distinguished-point rho at its largest instances — 0.24 was 0.21 at N = 224 on the conservative accounting — but only genus 4 has a fitted exponent behind it. Genus 3’s exponent claim was withdrawn once the linear algebra was priced. That is a toy-size result (p ≤ 251) whose reference needed correcting, not a statement about any deployed curve. The newer binary-field solver, the Crossbred decomposition oracle, the WDSat Riemann-Roch panel, the Weil-descent SAT round on the challenge curve and the parameter-sweep pilots are explicitly uncalibrated: their component counts do not establish an end-to-end speedup or belong in that normalized claim.

    The unit
    S = ops / √n

    Group operations per square root of the group order, so rho is flat at every size. Counted end to end across every phase — setup, relation finding, the decomposition oracle and linear algebra — with non-addition counters converted at ratios pinned in the repository rather than measured per run, because end-to-end speed is the measure of speed: a phase-only crossover is a diagnostic, not a win.

    Boundary 1 · the floors
    S ≥ √(π/2A)

    A generic algorithm needs √(πn/2A) operations with A automorphisms: 0.886 with negation, √(π/4n) on a Koblitz curve. The residual-walk panels use the count floor κ ≥ √(2(B+1)/γ).

    Boundary 2 · the reference
    rho, counted

    S ≈ 1.3 on E(Fp3) with the residual-walk accounting. On the three-regime ledger, matched to the curve’s automorphisms with the setup inside: 0.97 to 3.6 on the prime and binary ladders (the negation-map walk, walk alone 0.87 to 1.6; the plain walk they were priced against until §18 read 2.3 to 23), 0.20 to 19 on the Koblitz ladder (signed Frobenius, canonicalisation unpriced). For a figure that solves 32 targets together, batch rho at k = 32 on the same curve: 0.022–0.030 a target (§19). On current main, over nine sizes, it is 0.98–4.5× its floor, counted, and a canonical step prices at 1.8–2.3 units (§20).

    Closest to rho, one target
    5.2× cold at 236.6 §23: 4.9×

    The Koblitz collection thread on one unseen point, set-up and online together, against rho on the same point, at baseline v3 (rule v3, 2026-10-06; §23 measured v0). Online alone it is 10.2–26.5× faster (§23: 8.8–17.5×), but the set-up that buys that would serve a generic walk as precomputation too. Rho priced at the canonical step makes this 9.1× (§23: 8.6×). Both arms gained here since §23, so the ratio barely moved; at the three largest sizes it fell, from 14.7, 15.7 and 31.6× to 13.2, 12.0 and 21.0×. §23’s 2.0× at 238.0 was bound by a curve construction both arms paid, longer than rho’s walk; round 3 made it 1.28 ms, and v3 reads 6.1× there. Before the rule, operation-counted and now legacy diagnostics: meet in the middle, m = 2, prime field, folded table, walked targets and a base at the family optimum (222 signed points against the rule’s 512), was 13.5× at 223.4 against the matched negation-map rho (3.55× against the plain walk, 3.63× in Round 4). Amortised over 32 targets, the Koblitz thread was 3.62× batch rho at best (§22; 4.28× in §21, 4.86× in §20, 6.5× in §19), and one target alone §20 measured it at 22.6× there.

    Boundary 3 · the family’s own floor
    S ≥ 0.75 (#E t/k)2/3/(t√r)

    What the best member of the pair-table family costs at any base size, with t the table fold and k the column fold. A model of that family, not a bound on the problem — its relation term counts K/2 edges, and a multigraph closes earlier — so a row may sit under it. On a prime-order curve it is Θ(r1/6) where the reference is flat, which is the round’s result — measured at r[0.13, 0.19] across three certified cells spanning 1100× in r, each at its own swept base — against the tournament worker’s rho, which the triple-counted control found unmatched. Against batch rho, the Koblitz collection thread fits r0.137 [−0.06, 0.33] over its four largest sizes on current main (§22). §21 read r0.165 [0.010, 0.320] and §20 r0.137 [−0.10, 0.37].

    Curve by curve, with the best recipe on each, its phase split and its ratio to the matched reference: the index-calculus leaderboard; the question, the answer so far and what is open and closed, in one page that links back here: where things stand. Every curve on any of these pages is named by its ICV1 slug (docs/curves/ICV1.md).

    Three regimes on one axis

    Prices every index-calculus variant across three curve regimes against the generic floor and a matched rho reference, with every logarithm verified and the Koblitz vs rho figure an upper bound.

    A generic prime-field curve, a random binary curve and a Koblitz curve, each solving the same planted logarithm end to end with every phase inside the count — factor base, targets, decomposition oracle, pair table, elimination, verification — priced in group-addition equivalents per √r against the generic floor √(π/2A) and a counted Pollard rho on the same instance. Native counts are exact; since Round 4 the conversion factors are ratios pinned in docs/ic/calibration.json, not re-measured on the host each run, and both are stored in the run. Rows are the largest instance of each regime, plus the largest Koblitz rung on which the control was run; the full ladder and the fits are in research/notes/index-calculus/RESEARCH_IC_BOUNDARY_LEDGER.md. The second round (that note’s §10) keeps every first-round row as the before mark of the rung built on it and adds the rungs of a cumulative engineering ledger — the pair table folded by negation, then (Koblitz) by the Frobenius, targets drawn by an r-adding walk, two-summand rows where the cofactor classes admit them, and a Koblitz base sized to the folded table — each priced with every phase inside, on the same curves, targets and seeds. The third round (§11) makes the walk’s restart cost one group operation instead of thirty-two scalar multiplications, gives the prime and binary ladders a base at the family optimum, and derives the shape law of the whole family: a two-summand row pays F²/4t for its table and about c·#E/(2kF) for its relations, least at F = (c·#E·t/k)1/3, which in this unit is 0.75(#E·t/k)2/3/(t√r) — unbounded in r where the reference is flat. The vs family column is each row’s distance from that optimum at its own folds. The fifth round (§13) draws the walk’s sixteen restart offsets on first use instead of at setup: 110 of Round 4’s 204 walk rows had bought all sixteen and taken none. Because the offsets come off their own random stream and are taken in a fixed cycle, the before and after walk bit-identical trajectories, so the saving is a subtraction rather than an estimate — 537 of 537 rows identical in every counter but the pool’s, zero trajectories moved, zero rows whose saving differs from the offsets they stopped drawing.

    P-256 S17 boundary, corrected for the finite representation domain. This route is not a fourth comparable whole-pipeline row: it has no recovered public logarithm. Round 18 rejected fixed-atom enumeration at 2272.404 field multiplications; Round 19’s exact global 8+9 frontier lowered that to 2165.156. Round 20 initially reported 2144.625, but that symmetric projection demanded 2136.538 distinct left images from a domain containing only 2128.734 and is withdrawn. Materialising the complete finite left domain and charging streamed right images plus duplicate occupancy gives 2151.885 P-256 field-multiplication equivalents, 19.419 bits above rho. Round 21 exhausts 14,399,656 exact small-multiple and Dickson-block images without finding one cross-column relation. Rounds 22 and 23 extend the exact census to 26 geometric bases and 55,089,792 multiplier images with zero cross-column hits. Their 494.475× and 491.494× projections are superseded: Round 24 proves that both equal and opposite cross-colour orientations replay, then applies the exact K-th collision law on the negation quotient. The corrected selected-base boundary is 394.533× rho; the best root-orbit base is 392.155×. A known-log K=1 control reaches an ideal 0.964×-rho collision constant, but direct generation is 7.715× rho, one-list storage is 2133.326 bytes, and a memoryless implementation is rho-equivalent. These remain rejected stage projections and are not inserted into the end-to-end table.

    Frozen source: docs/ic/runs/ic-boundary-ledger-round5-2026-09-22.json (ic boundary --oracles). Means over three targets; rho over eight walks per target. Every logarithm on the board recovered and verified as [d]G = Q. The prime and binary references are the matched negation-map walk (A = 2) on the same seeds and targets, re-priced in ledger §18 (research/ic_rho_reference_20260923/reprice/): each “vs rho” reads against it, with the plain walk’s figure as “was”. The Koblitz reference and floor use all 2n signed-Frobenius automorphisms; that reference prices its per-step canonicalisation at zero (§18.8), so its “vs rho” is an upper bound, by about 1.07× at n = 41.

Drawn lazily, 155 of 204 rows draw fewer, and the saving is exactly (48 log₂r − 48)/√r to within 1–9% — so it is large below 215 (best ratio 0.58) and small above 220 (best 0.93, at Koblitz 222, where S is lowest; 1.000 on all three rows of this panel).     The reference, matched: rho with the negation map accounting

Through §17 the prime and binary rows on this page, and every ic bench row, divided by a plain walk that used no automorphism and paid most of its S in setup: two scalar multiplications per walk start, a 560-operation table, and walks long enough that about one in fifty cycled without a distinguished point and ran to its cap.     The Koblitz descent’s fixed cost, per target engineering

    Batches walk starts and does relation arithmetic in machine words, an engineering change measured in isolated runs that speeds the smaller sizes up to 1.392x and leaves the largest sizes flat.

    Ledger §22. After §21 the descent was the largest phase at six of nine sizes. Below 237 a target needs few probes, so it was paying fixed cost: 64 walk starts made one addition at a time, a relation turned into its logarithm in big-integer arithmetic, and the recovery check. The candidate batches the walk starts off precomputed stride multiples, and does the relation’s arithmetic modulo r in machine words. It also makes the solver’s own check in single words. Every walk, trial and logarithm is unchanged. Declared before any candidate code, and measured on §20’s 36 frozen files against current main: five rounds interleaved on one thread, counts and logarithms pinned in all 186 pairs. Every timed process ran through tools/isolated_bench.py (AGENTS.md §10). One of 481 was contended and was run again, and none failed. A first run pinned with taskset alone is kept, but it is not evidence. Because the unit moves between binaries (§21.4), the declared speedup puts both arms at one unit: the paired ratio of time. Frozen source: research/ic_descent_20260930/ (analysis-isolated.json for every figure here). Its ratios to rho are k = 32 figures, historical multi-target diagnostics since #1076; the one-target comparison is §23.

    One unseen point, online and cold accounting

    Measures index calculus against rho on one unseen point per process, finding index calculus faster online at all six sizes but rho faster cold at all six, with 408 claims verified.

    Ledger §23. AGENTS.md’s IC measurement rules (#1076) make the primary comparison one previously unseen target. The index calculus and rho run on the same point, in one process. Each is timed from its first target-dependent operation to a checked logarithm, and the reusable set-up is reported apart. At the thread’s six largest sizes, 64 public hash-to-curve points per size ran one isolated process each. Every row is keyed by its canonical identities, and both answers are replayed outside the process. All 408 claims pass the repository’s vs_rho checker. Rho is the tuned signed-Frobenius walk with its walks batched (ParallelRho); its only set-up is its jump table, in G. The round was declared before any run, and §23’s earlier k = 32 declaration was withdrawn unrun. Frozen source: research/ic_single_target_20260930/ (analysis.json for every figure here).

    S is units over √r, each row in its own process’s unit, the mean over 64 targets per size. Online speedup: mean rho online over mean index-calculus online, with a 95% bootstrap interval over targets. Canonical step: rho’s counted operations priced at the canonical step, the conservative reading. Cold: set-up plus online, index calculus over rho. Break-even: the count of targets at which one set-up and their descents cost as much as as many one-target rho runs. BL model: the index calculus’s online cost over the online cost of a generic walk given the same set-up as precomputation (Bernstein–Lange; a model). A/A: four targets’ second process over their first.

    The ic tool programme, baseline by baseline engineering

    Tracks ic tool cold speed against frozen baselines: Round 3's construction fix and Round 5's presence filter accepted as baselines, the wide-kernel round rejected on its holdout and its re-test withdrawn on v3, and Round 7 re-basing the programme on main's head as v3, where the rule's comparison leaves rho 5.2-21.0x faster cold; Rounds 6 and 8 are declared and wait for a host of their class.

    The programme makes the ic tool faster, round after round, against frozen baselines (plan, #1103). “Faster” means faster than its previous baseline, end to end and cold, with identical outputs. Each round is declared before its runs.

    • The suite (v1) is eleven Koblitz curves from 218 to 247.2, each with four recipe seeds and two public targets.
    • Round 1 (v0) pinned main against §23, profiled every phase on the suite and measured the noise floor, all in isolated runs. The pin held on all 12 shared rows, so §23’s single-target figures are v0’s.
    • Round 2 (rejected) gave the AVX-512 batched addition the two fields whose polynomial has n + deg t = 66. Collection ran 1.29–1.31× faster there and cold time 1.18–1.27×, with identical outputs. Its declared rule asked for a lower end above 1.10 on the suite and on the holdouts separately, and the ten-pair holdout at 244.5 missed it.
    • Round 4 (a stage diagnostic, run before round 3) timed each stage of the collection scan, with probes compiled into a separate build. At three of the four largest sizes the batched subtraction holds the most scan time, 37–41%; at 244.3 the admitted keys hold 42%. The probes’ overhead interval fell inside R01’s A/A band at no size, so these shares are reported, not trusted.
    • Round 3 (baseline v1) made the curve’s construction test primality only when a division changes what is left. At 238.0, a composite degree, the construction fell from 56.0 to 1.28 ms and cold time ran 1.771× [1.694, 1.851] faster on the suite and 1.922× [1.756, 2.104] on the holdouts, with every pinned output v0’s. It is the first baseline after v0.
    • Round 5 (baseline v2) made the presence filter set three bits a key in one 64-bit word, at eight to sixteen bits a stored pair, so a probe still reads one word. At the three largest sizes collection ran 1.36–1.52× faster, and cold time 1.293× [1.270, 1.317], 1.238× [1.215, 1.262] and 1.303× [1.281, 1.324] faster on the suite and 1.276×, 1.240× and 1.319× on fresh holdouts, with every pinned output v0’s.
    • Round 7 (baseline v3) re-based the programme on main’s head, 995ea207, which carries v1’s and v2’s code and about 700 later commits, among them #1242’s carry-less folds for every field product. It was accepted on its pin and its own A/A bands, with no minimum gain. Cold time ran 1.135× [1.104, 1.167], 1.483× [1.452, 1.514] and 1.526× [1.507, 1.546] faster than v2 at the three largest sizes, 1.170×, 1.483× and 1.539× on fresh holdouts, and 1.110–1.287× at the eight other sizes, with every pinned output v0’s. The gain is main’s, not a lever of the programme’s. It is the newest baseline.
    • The rule at v3 re-ran §23’s single-target comparison on v3: the same six sizes, 64 targets and four A/A repeats a size, 408 of 408 rows checked and every logarithm §23’s. Online the index calculus is 10.2–26.5× faster than rho on the same point (§23: 8.8–17.5×). Cold, with its set-up, it costs 5.2–21.0× rho’s (§23: 2.0–31.6×), so rho is still faster at every size, and the gap grows as r0.18 [0.14, 0.21].

    Where the set-up goes. The cold cost is the set-up, and the online interval is 0.1–2% of it. From 232 up, collection is the largest phase, at 41–89% of the set-up. The exception is 238.0, where the curve’s construction takes 45%. A scanned summand costs 1.36–1.49 units from 236.6 up, but 2.17–2.18 at the two sizes whose field polynomial has n + deg t = 66. The AVX-512 batched addition refuses those two fields, and round 2 tests whether that is the cause. The noise floor. v0 against a byte-identical copy reads within ±4–11% in cold time at ten pairs per size. One interval excludes 1: 1.075 [1.005, 1.149] at 239.0. A ratio inside the band is not a gain. Huge pages are not a lever through glibc’s tunable. Cold time reads 0.96–1.00× at the three largest sizes. Collection gains 5–12%, but the build loses up to 1.5× and system time rises 3–5×. This host’s memory costs 44–70 ns per random access from 2 to 32 MiB and 221 ns at 256 MiB. Round 2, graded. The control held: switching the AVX-512 scan kernels off made collection 1.89× slower per summand at 244.3. Every output of both arms equals v0’s on all 90 rows. At 244.5 the suite reads 1.182 [1.151, 1.213] and the holdouts 1.161 [1.089, 1.239]; at 247.2, 1.267 [1.242, 1.292] and 1.262 [1.216, 1.310]. The predictions were 1.31× and 1.37×: a wide field’s summand costs 1.90–1.95 units with the kernel, not the 1.6 assumed, and the build did not move. The nine other sizes read 0.973–1.027×, inside their A/A bands. The callgrind control failed too: under valgrind both arms take the portable paths, and the candidate’s ran 0.1% fewer instructions, all in the compiler’s code for two scan functions it does not change. Runs hours apart differ. v0 against v0′, interleaved in R02’s session, reads 0.97–1.07× in cold time: the renaming between them moved nothing. Yet v0′’s S in R02’s runs sits 4–16% above v0’s in R01’s at the six sizes above, on the same host. Only the paired ratio compares across rounds; S between runs carries the host’s drift. Likewise, v1’s S in round 5’s runs sits 1–11% above its S in round 3’s. Round 4, the scan’s stages. At 244.5 and 247.2 the subtraction costs 32.5 and 33.3 ns a summand, against 13.1 at 244.3, where the 8-lane kernel runs. That was round 2’s target. On v3 the premium is gone: R04’s probes on main’s head put the subtraction at 11.3 and 12.1 ns there and the whole scan at 35–36 ns a summand, about a third each for the subtraction, the key, and the filter with the admitted keys. A check made after the run, not declared: the presence filter is one bit per stored pair under one hash, and from 236.6 up its predicted pass rate matches the admitted fraction to within 2%. Nearly every admitted key is a false positive, at 118–159 ns each at the three largest sizes. Round 5 then tested a filter of three bits a key in one word, and made v2. Round 3, graded. Every pinned output equals v0’s on all 90 rows. At 238.0 the suite reads 1.771 [1.694, 1.851] and the holdouts 1.922 [1.756, 2.104], against a predicted 1.75×. At 224.8, the other composite degree, it reads 1.007 [0.985, 1.030] against a predicted 1.3×: that order’s cofactor ends at 211, so the old loop was short there. The nine prime sizes read 0.970–1.049×, every interval overlapping its A/A band. The construction stage is under 2.2 ms everywhere, but at the prime sizes it was already a few milliseconds of a set-up of seconds. Round 5, graded. Every pinned output equals v0’s on all 90 rows. At the three largest sizes a scanned summand falls from 1.80, 2.55 and 2.56 units to 1.18, 1.87 and 1.88, and collection runs 1.522, 1.371 and 1.356× faster, against a model’s 1.551, 1.385 and 1.397×. Cold time came in 1–3% under the model, which left out the larger filter’s own cost. The online interval gains too, 1.25–1.34×, because its descent probes the same filter; rho’s does not move, 0.985–1.005×. At the two smallest sizes cold time reads 0.939 and 0.933, each interval overlapping its A/A band; collection did not move there, and rho’s online interval, which the patch does not change, reads 0.936 and 0.948 in the same pairs. The container was rebuilt during the holdouts, which finished on the native runner. Round 7, graded. Main’s head against v2, read in this host’s own A/A bands, since its kernel build is not R01’s. Every output equals v0’s on all 90 rows, and the A/A reads 0.988–1.043. At the two sizes whose polynomial has n + deg t = 66, a scanned summand falls from 1.85 and 1.80 units to 1.15 and 1.14, the 8-lane kernel’s cost: #1242’s carry-less folds made each scalar product about 2.4× cheaper, closing the gap round 2 and R02b chased with a kernel. 244.3, whose scan already ran that kernel, gains least, 1.135×. Rho’s online interval is 1.11–1.82× faster too, so the ratio to rho waits for the rule’s comparison at v3. Under callgrind, on the portable paths, main runs 27–29% fewer instructions, and both arms recover the same logarithm. The container restarted three times, and each resume found the same host class. R02b, withdrawn. Its go/no-go on v3, declared in its amendment 3, ran main’s head against main’s head plus round 2’s kernel. Cold time read 0.962 [0.865, 1.069] at 244.5 and 0.918 [0.858, 0.982] at 247.2, base over candidate, on five clean pairs each. The kernel now loses to main’s scalar path, and collection is 12% and 8% slower with it. That is below its 1.05 rule at both sizes, so R02b was withdrawn without running and the kernel retired; it counts as neither an acceptance nor a failed round. The rule at v3. The cold ratio to rho fell at the three largest sizes, from 14.7, 15.7 and 31.6× to 13.2, 12.0 and 21.0×, where R05’s filter and main’s folds made the set-up cheaper. At 236.6 and 239.0 it barely moved, 4.95 to 5.23 and 8.04 to 7.66×, because rho’s walk gained as much. At 238.0 it rose from 1.98 to 6.12×: §23’s figure was bound by a curve construction both arms paid, which round 3 made 1.28 ms. Every target’s online speedup is above 1; with rho at the canonical step it is 4.55–13.3×, and by Bernstein and Lange’s trade-off, a model, a generic walk given the same set-up would still be 1.42–3.52× faster online (§23: 2.0–8.0). The comparison’s rho takes 0.50–0.62 of the strong walk’s time a step, so the reference is admissible. Fitted over the six sizes, the cold ratio grows as r0.18 [0.14, 0.21]; §23’s r0.30 included the construction-bound point, so the two are not like for like. Declared, not yet run: R06 and R08. R06 changes the scan’s key (GFNI and funnel shifts) and R08 its subtraction (two carry-less folds a product, eight lanes, with the negated base as coordinate slices), each with the same outputs by construction. R08’s exploration on R06’s candidate read 1.293, 1.223 and 1.362 in cold time at the three largest sizes, with the subtraction at 4.7–4.9 ns a summand against v3’s 11.3–12.1. Neither is a measurement until its round runs. Both need the reference class, and on 2026-10-07 the container moved to a Cascade Lake host without GFNI, VBMI2 or VPCLMULQDQ, so R06 waits for a host of its class, and icprog now refuses a round’s timed steps outside its class. Declared on this host’s class, running: R09. On the Cascade Lake host the scan’s subtraction is the scalar product at every size, and a scanned summand costs 38–41 ns: 15.3–15.5 to subtract, 12.0–13.7 to key (stage diagnostic). R09 keys each rest from its slope, c + rotl(c) + d + e with c = coords(λ), so the squaring, the abscissa and its store go for every summand the filter rejects; it adds eight inversion chains, a cheaper rotation step, a run’s scans in three stages, and the build keyed the same way, with the same keys. Its exploration read 1.119 [1.093, 1.146], 1.112 [1.060, 1.166] and 1.103 [1.071, 1.136] in cold time at the three largest sizes, eight pairs each, every logarithm v3’s; it is not a measurement until the round runs. Its class is its own: AVX-512F and PCLMULQDQ without VPCLMULQDQ. Pipelining alone and A2 re-checked there moved cold time by nothing reliable. Explored, not declared. Huge pages advised on the pair tables (A2) halve the minor faults and leave cold time where it was, 0.960–1.068: the scan’s misses are cache misses. On R08’s candidate, the build’s partition streams and per-run filters (A1) make the build 1.40–1.47× faster, and prefetching each admitted key’s run (A13) makes collection 1.12–1.29× faster; each reads 1.07–1.12× in cold time on two rows a size. These are explorations, to be declared on the baseline R08 decides. accounting v0 is a baseline, not a change. Round 2 would have been engineering; it is rejected, and the kernel is kept on record as candidate.patch. Round 4 is accounting, a stage diagnostic: it changed no timed code, and nothing in it is a speedup. Round 3 is engineering: the factors are identical, so the ratio to the floor is flat. Round 5 is engineering: nothing the pipeline decides changes, so the ratio to the floor is flat. Round 7 is engineering, credited to main: every pinned output is v0’s, so the ratio to the floor is flat, and v3 is the newest baseline. The rule at v3 is accounting: it re-measures the comparison at the newest baseline and changes no algorithm.

    The exponents, per regime

    Lists fitted cost exponents for every variant on each ladder against rho's one half, with the matched rho reference reading 0.39 on binary and 0.37 on prime curves.

    Fitted growth of the whole cost in the subgroup order over each ladder, ops ∝ rα, from the run’s fits. Rho’s one half is the reference mark; its measured 0.37–0.39 on the prime and binary ladders (the matched walk, §18; 0.27–0.30 with the plain walk) and 0.25 on the Koblitz ladder is its unamortised setup. Anything to the right of one half loses as the group grows, whatever its constant.

    The P-256 S17 diagnostics are intentionally not plotted on this group-order axis. Round 18 measures a fixed-atom depth-prefix slope; Round 19 measures local B=17..20 list growth, with slopes 11.650 and 11.684 against log B. Round 20 measures a projected-key birthday ladder whose counted-work slope is 0.499979 per key bit and whose logical-memory slope is 0.5; none is a multi-size exponent in subgroup order. Its initial symmetric 2144.625 projection is withdrawn because it exceeds the signed-eight domain. Corrected finite-domain accounting projects the collector to 2151.885 FME, 19.419 bits above rho, while its optimistic image floor remains 16.203 bits above rho. Rounds 21–23 are exact fixed-P-256 transport censuses, not size ladders: the selected Dickson base, its nine earlier alternatives, and all sixteen PGL2 root-orbit bases retain their full quotient dimensions. Round 24 supersedes the 494.475× and 491.494× projections with the exact K-th collision law on the negation quotient: 394.533× for the selected base and 392.155× for the best-width root orbit. The ideal known-log K=1 constant is 0.964× rho, but its complete materialized/direct implementations fail and its memoryless form is rho-equivalent.

    Hamming ideals as a membership ideal for a Frobenius-stable weight base accounting

    Finds the membership-ideal oracle resolves only after nearly a whole summand is fixed and its call count outgrows the candidate count, so the negative result transfers and no operation count moves.

    Frozen source: research/hamming_ideal_pdp_20260930/results/main/summary.json (derived from the per-target records beside it; protocol and result in the same directory). A normal-basis weight-bounded base F_w = {P : wt_NB(x(P)) ≤ w} is Frobenius-stable at every prime n, needs no storage, and by La Scala–Marchesin–Tiwari has a bounded-degree membership ideal (C, FC, QFC). Their MultiSolve oracle, with a degree-truncated Boolean F4 inside, was run on K_0/F_2^n against the exhaustive oracle (|F_w| candidates per target) and a matched subspace base (SUB) through the same solver; MONO is the monomial-ideal control. Every target of every cell agrees with the exhaustive oracle. Unit: GroebnerSafe calls per target; the tame depth is the number of summand coordinates fixed before the basis became linear. No S, rho ratio or end-to-end figure: a stage diagnostic of one oracle, m = 2, w = 2.

    Verdict: the paper’s negative result on Classic McEliece transfers. The algebra resolves only after nearly a whole summand is fixed and the call count grows faster than the candidate count, so the oracle is the enumeration with a Gröbner computation attached to each candidate. What the construction changes is the decomposition note’s §6 storage term for a Frobenius-stable set (removed); no operation count moves, and the verdict at the top of this page is unchanged. Budget sensitivity: 16× the per-call budget lowers the tame depth by one to two levels at n = 11 (results/tau/TABLE.md).

    Verdict of the seven: the fold by any finite group of endomorphisms is the order of the subgroup of (Z/rZ)* that the group’s eigenvalues generate — the automorphism group’s roots of unity, the Frobenius’s, and their products, and no more — and the matched rho takes the square root of the same number. Nothing moved a ratio to a floor. Where the endomorphisms fix a cofactor (E5) the fold buys columns and not relations with two summands, and columns and relations with three (E8). The matched folded rho takes √(A/2) fewer steps on every group (E6, E9) and, in field multiplications, pays for each step’s canonicalisation. Against the literature (note §8.0): the invariant base is Galbraith–Granger–Merz–Petit’s lever measured at framework level; the Faugère–Gaudry–Huot–Renault symmetries act on the decomposition system, not the base, and the two multiply. The algebraic S₄ oracle (E11) makes the relation phase flat in p and the fold’s arm the first on this page with a fitted exponent below rho’s 1/2, (corrected, note §8.10: rho’s exponent is the best a line base can reach on these groups) at a constant of about 0.9 million multiplications a solve. The orbit-representative pair table (E12) shrinks the table by w/2 and is worth having only where the table is the cost (two summands on Fp, S ÷ 1.18 on j = 0); on the line it costs 2 %. A rational 2-torsion point (E13) is used twice and the two uses compound: as FGHR’s symmetry of the system it replaces a 64-dimensional quotient by a degree-16 resultant (S ÷ 27), and as a translation with eigenvalue 1 it folds the base 12 a column (S ÷ 2.5 more). The best arm on this panel is then 267× the matched rho, the solver three quarters of its cost; nothing moves an exponent, and nothing here is faster than rho. On the ECC2K-130 family (E15) the fold is unconfined at the challenge’s 4·prime shape (m = 23, D = 1), while m = 31 — the program’s primary exploratory size, which cannot have that shape — is confined by its 373 cofactor (73 % single-column rows). Q-curves of degree 2 and 3 over Fp² (E14) keep base points only at chance, as E4’s CM maps did, so the folds on these families are the automorphisms, the Frobenius-type maps and the 2-torsion translation; every experiment of §8.1 has run. E16 states the boundary that governs them: on a subfield curve the large prime lives in the trace-zero part, r ≈ p², so rho costs Θ(p) and no line base can do better than a constant; the best arm’s ratio to rho grows as r0.18 to p = 216.

    The grading is real — S₄ on a j = 0 curve is ψ-invariant term by term — but with x_R fixed every Macaulay row couples all three weight classes (100 % on every residual); the only object it grades is the orbit system, which has three times the solutions and 456 of its 648 Bézout solutions at infinity. Block-aware elimination never multiplies across blocks that a sparse-aware elimination would have multiplied anyway, so it is a footprint lever (3×) and not a field-operation lever (1.4–5 %). S is unchanged by everything in this panel.

The completed p = 59 census has 100,408 weak ordinary rows out of 201,898 and 540 higher-depth zero rows; all 5,000 controls agree. The persistent worker has advanced to p = 61. Measured controls, theorem, and receipts.

    ISO-1 norm-one theorem: every ordinary weak curve over an odd extension with q ≡ 1 (mod 4) has Frobenius conductor divisible by four. The exact p = 7 class t = ±610 has conductor 72 and no weak representative, certified by exhaustive field counts and every independent GP orbit. Absolute Frobenius and inversion reduce the cubic census to (p4+3p2+8)/12 point counts. The completed p = 53 census has 72,540 weak rows among 146,068 ordinary rows and 494 high-depth zero rows, with all 5,000 independent GP controls positive; p = 59 is running. Theorem and proof; census and continuation.

    The k = 4 Joux–Vitse row supersedes the derived “near 36× rho at every size” of §11.16, which borrowed C′ = 1,513 from the k = 3 pair test: the three-point test is four quartics in three unknowns, inconsistent with a certificate at degree 7 on an 84 × 117 matrix, and F4 spends 1.6·105 multiplications on it at every size (2,400 tests, 320 planted triples all found, 0 mismatches against the pair-table oracle). The ratio is flat as derived, and the constant is 193× the derivation. Class: a measurement of a derived route; relabelling of the k = 4 solve (C₄ moved into a p-fold residual count), no class for the boundary statement. Parity at a size that fits a machine needs a route this harness does not have — k ≥ 5 with torsion symmetries, or a cover — and the note registered the first before building it. Built and measured (the three k = 5 rows): the 2-torsion symmetry cuts the four-point test 416×, to 7.3·107 multiplications, and the route still crosses rho only at 2233 (the first round said 2203 on a residual rate it had not counted; the census counts it, 8× lower). The second round built the 4-torsion variant and retracted it as a lever: no degree halves, and saturating the residual over the four translates is a wash. The one lever left (a trace-driven elimination, 3–10×) is priced in RESEARCH_K5_TORSION_JOUX_VITSE.md §5; it does not reach 2200. The last row is the one route in the ledger whose measured S / rho falls at a polynomial rate to a crossover inside an extrapolation (267); it is a published algorithm reproduced on a weak class of curves (class: accounting and engineering, no advance), and it was built after four defects the oracle and the registered predictions caught (RESEARCH_COVER_DECOMPOSITION_LEDGER.md §8).

    Where the programme stands. On the generic curves of this harness no measured route reaches parity below 2150: k = 3 is bounded by exponents, k = 4 Joux–Vitse by a constant (6,945×), the routes that close do so past 2151 (k = 4 full) and 2233 (k = 5), and the registered 4-torsion lever does not exist. The cover route closes by a polynomial, S / rho ∝ n−0.32, to about 9× at 258 and an extrapolated parity near 267 (5–6× and 265 once F4 is stopped at the Bézout staircase, a 1.61× constant on the test, class engineering) — on a weak class of curves, with the isogeny walk priced at a walk of q/3 steps of 3–7·105 multiplications (above rho below p ≈ 8,000; §13), then rebuilt in §17: about 1 % of the route for a curve whose class holds a weak curve, and 60.8 % of random full-2-torsion curves are estimated to be in such a class at p = 37 (corrected census; Wilson 95 % interval 59.3–62.3 %; the historical p ≤ 31 values were superseded). Nothing here is a new algorithm or a statement about a deployed curve (RESEARCH_RHO_PARITY_PROGRAMME.md §8).

    All 54 trace fibers have positive mass in every larger base: no whole-target rejection from this quotient. At 30 bits, the prefix d10 success ceiling is 15.896911%, not a measured success rate. Under uniform targets, full base scans and a linear number of required relation rows, explicit pair setup plus queries has the conditional lower bound Omega(M^2 + N/M).     What was actually found

    Three regimes now share one axis. A generic prime-field curve, a random binary curve and a Koblitz curve solve the same planted logarithm with every phase counted. A second round of engineering — the pair table folded by negation and, on Koblitz curves, by the Frobenius; targets drawn by an r-adding walk instead of two scalar multiplications each; two-summand rows wherever the cofactor classes admit them; a Koblitz base sized to the folded table — takes the best rows to 6.2×, 31× and 26× the counted rho (the prime and binary figures against the plain walk they were priced against then; the matched walk of ledger §18 reads them 2.4–3.8× higher), worth 1.3–2.9× per instance on the prime and binary ladders and 3–49× on the Koblitz one. Nothing crosses rho and no fitted exponent falls below the reference's, so every rung is engineering, not an advance. The counting ceiling is now computed exactly from the base's cofactor classes rather than argued: the index it corrects for is 1.9–2.2 on the trace-zero bases, 3.0 at n = 15 and 4.6 at n = 29.

    A collision was being counted as a relation. A run that decomposes the same group element twice gets two rows with one factor-base part and different coefficients, and those pin the logarithm by themselves — a generic collision resolved through the factor base, arriving after about √r targets whatever the oracle costs. Measured: 24.4% of unguarded two-summand runs end that way, which is the predicted K²/(2rp) = 1/4, and 82% when walk segments share one jump table and merge as rho's walks do. Both target sources are now guarded, which costs 1.1–2.9× in S on the affected rows and moved 22 of the first round's 63 rows by up to 1.59×. The first-round figures on this page are the corrected ones (research/notes/index-calculus/RESEARCH_IC_BOUNDARY_LEDGER.md §10.2).

    The walk hypothesis is closed. Collision search over partial decompositions cannot beat independent sampling, because the relation yield is bounded by a counting argument. Every lever tried left the ratio to that floor between 1.00 and 1.07.

    Published constants are soft. The three-unknown solve lost a factor of 5.5 to ordinary linear algebra, worth fifteen bits of crossover. If the same slack exists elsewhere, quoted crossover sizes are optimistic.

    The n4/9 is real. Measured 0.44 against the predicted 0.444, end to end, every run recovering the planted logarithm.

    The 2/3 is exact too. Pair-only decompositions were predicted to need n2/3 residuals at k = 3; measured 0.666 over four sizes, the cleanest confirmation of a predicted exponent on this board.

    One diagnosis on this board was wrong. The residuals no Macaulay degree closes were recorded as having solutions at infinity, fixable by saturation. Measured, the ideal is zero-dimensional, the affine variety carries one F_p-point where a positive- dimensional component would carry about p, and a generic change of coordinates rescued none of 28. It is the staircase border meeting the degree cut — a truncation artefact, so the fix is a border basis, not saturation. The fixed-staircase border basis built in §11.14 does not reach them: their staircase is not the generic one (dimension 61 at degree 10), so no per-curve plan serves them. Whether Mourrain's full iteration would is untested.

    Where the boundaries bite

    The plain method never wins. Relations cost n1/3 and its linear algebra n0.68, so cost bottoms out near 200× rho around 250 and rises after. No reduction in the solve constant changes that.

    The large-prime variant wins too late. Its score falls as n−1/18, so closing the measured factor of 1,987 takes roughly two hundred doublings of the group order.

    The loose end is closed, and the missing piece does not fit. This panel said row weight doubling pushes the large-prime linear algebra to n0.56 and that “capping the merge level is the missing piece”. The cap was built and measured over six seeds, paired so each seed is its own control — the fitted exponent moves by 0.04 between seeds, which is the size of the whole effect, and a two-seed version of this comparison said the opposite of the truth. At k = 12 the solve exponent falls 0.045 ± 0.017 (2.6σ, five seeds of six) and row weight at p = 2083 drops 20.93 → 11.89, exactly as intended — and the eliminator's own work rises 0.043 ± 0.030, cancelling it, so the linear algebra as a whole moves −0.009 ± 0.019, which is nothing. End to end the cap is worse, +0.051 ± 0.031 on five seeds of six. Its cost is not the 0.3–2% of relations it discards but the full relations that never form: yield per residual falls to 0.64× at the two largest sizes against 0.95× at the smallest, and a yield loss that grows in n is a residual exponent that rises. Mean merge depth is flat across the ladder, so chains are not lengthening — the tail past the cap thickens. Class engineering, negative; S is untouched, as the pre-registration said in advance it would be (experiments/22_gaudry_merge_cap_uncapped.json, …_k12.json; §§11.10–11.11).

    And the exponent it was built to fix was never pinned. The n0.56 above is a two-seed figure quoted without an error bar. Six seeds give 0.516 ± 0.027 — still 2.7σ above 4/9, so the concern was real — and 0.56 sits inside a two-seed ±0.046. Meanwhile the end-to-end exponent is 0.424 ± 0.016, consistent with 4/9: the large-prime variant does reach n4/9 over this ladder, because its linear algebra is about 2% of the cost. The higher linear-algebra exponent bites only near 298, and capping the merge level is not how to meet it there.

    A bigger field is not a lever. Base-changing ECC2K-130 to F2131e leaves the target group and its 262 automorphisms untouched, so the reference stays 260.81 at every e. Because 131 is prime, every subfield and every Frobenius-stable subspace of that field is either of dimension ≥ 130 — a 2131 factor base, 270.19× rho at the cheapest e and rising with e — or contained in F2e, where the factor base lies inside the subgroup E(F2e) and no relation exists at any cost. Checked for e = 1…16; embedding degree > 107 closes the transfer route (experiments/ecc2k130_extension_field_boundary.json).

    A bigger genus is not a lever either. A cover over F2131 is priced by that field, so the cheapest one, genus 2, costs 2131 — 270.19× rho, the same row as the bigger field. Over F2, the only proper subfield, index calculus would be cheap: genus 130 would cost 237.17, 223.64× below the reference, and it pays up to genus 290–300. No construction lands there. Because 2 is a primitive root mod 131, GHS descent gives every curve over F2131 genus 1, 2129 or 2130, and at genus 1 the transfer is exactly the zero map on the target subgroup. The best explicit curve carrying the subgroup is the modular curve XH(3²·7²·263²) mod 2, at genus 508,799,809 ≈ 228.92 — 220.69 above the window, with index calculus on it astronomically above rho. Every geometrically cyclic degree-131 cover of a curve of genus ≤ 1 needs genus ≥ 1300 (2148.92 under the exact model, 288.11× rho). Correction, accounting: this paragraph said the nearest available genus was 2120.77 away; that is the gap to GHS descent, not to every construction (experiments/ecc2k130_hyperelliptic_cover_boundary.json, research/notes/ecc2k130/curve_construction_20261006/results/curve_construction.json).

    Homogeneous relations do not exist to be found. Complete three-point sweeps over the weight-two support and its variants, every pair of every base, found 0 relations on the 4,262-point weight-two support (2−95.4 predicted) and 0 on its 1,090-point σ-stable subset (2−101.3). The one hit, on the 4,336-point weight-at-most-two support, is degenerate. Four-point, orbit-grouped: eight normal bases swept to completion, 1,020,114 pair-orbits (227.0 signed pairs), 490 candidates, 0 certified against an expectation of 2−79.4. All 490 candidates are instances of σ2 + σ + 2 = 0 — exactly 2 per lifting orbit — so the search recovers the endomorphism ring’s own identity and nothing else. Every yield matches the counting prediction; no support evades the floor (research/ecc2k130_relations/results/summary.json, four_point_orbit_summary.json).

    Frobenius is a real saving and not a lever. On a normal basis the weight-two support is closed under σ, so the stored side of the meet-in-the-middle holds one canonical class per orbit and a 131 × T-point support carries only T unknowns. Applied at every m it is worth 216.1–218.4, more at larger m, so it does not change which m is cheapest — it changes the margin (four_point_orbit_boundary.json).

    Extended past m = 8 the homogeneous table crosses rho, and that is the trap. Continuing the quotiented self-consistent accounting, it goes sub-reference at m = 18 and reaches 2−4.05 at m = 28. Those rows price relations among base points alone, which give one linear equation among unknown logarithms and determine logP(Q) not at all.

    Priced as a logarithm, the gap is 2+6.48 and every step of it is bookkeeping. T + 1 relations against known targets [a]P + [b]Q, the meet-in-the-middle table built once, probes and their canonicalisation priced in rho’s own unit, memory charged at zero. One table, one unit (S = operations / √r, √r = 264.5):
